protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording: an authorised pharmacist on the register of authorised pharmacists prescribing in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code (p2). Discretion clause (p6): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.' Pharmacotherapy delegated to external references (p12): oral analgesia per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharmacological management of acute pain; oral antibiotic therapy per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Ear, nose and throat infections – Otitis media), with NB1/NB2/NB3 notes (p12-p13). Shared decision-making on antibiotics is required (NB1, p13).
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist assessment and management of acute otitis media (AOM). Service restricted to patients aged 2 years or over. Covers 'Red flag' warning signs necessitating referral to emergency medical care ('Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000' including suspected meningitis and fever/hypothermia with sepsis signs; 'Urgent referral to an emergency department (without concurrent antibiotic therapy)'), referral to a general practitioner ('Urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours' with and without concurrent antibiotic therapy), key points, patient history, examination and pneumatic otoscopy (TM must be visualised to confirm diagnosis), complications of AOM (Table 1 high-risk children), management and treatment plan (supportive management, aural hygiene, dry mopping, oral analgesia, oral antibiotic therapy per NB3 with mandatory concurrent referral when antibiotics are prescribed), confirmation of management, communication of the agreed management plan, patient resources, general advice and prevention, and clinical review (3 months intact TM; 4-6 weeks small perforation). 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

diagnosis_pathways.name: Assessment and management of acute otitis media

steps.description: Gather information and assess patient's needs: 'In both children and adults, the diagnosis of AOM is based on clinical history and ear examination using a pneumatic otoscope (1, 3, 5, 6).' 'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' The patient history should consider: age; whether the patient identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander; social history, including identifying if the patient belongs to a vulnerable population, arrangements for supporting management at home, ability to access further care and capacity to undertake appropriate self-care, and whether the patient is under guardianship or out-of-home care arrangements (8); nature, severity and frequency of symptoms including pain, itch, discharge, hearing loss, a feeling of fullness, tinnitus and dizziness/vertigo; onset and duration of symptoms including preceding illnesses; precipitating and relieving factors; medication and other strategies tried to treat current symptoms; recent history of URTI; other presenting symptoms including temperature > 38°C or < 35.5°C, rash, increased respiratory rate/distress, dehydration and/or reduced urine output, runny nose, sore throat or cough; family history of ear conditions and hearing loss; previous history of AOE, OM or other ear conditions (hearing loss and recent hearing tests; patient age at first episode of ear conditions; under the care of an ENT specialist or audiologist; ear surgery, current or previous tympanostomy tubes (grommets)); underlying medical conditions, e.g., immunocompromised (including diabetes), cochlear implant, craniofacial abnormalities, persistent hearing loss, that mean the patient is at high risk of experiencing AOM complications (refer to Table 1); delayed speech or language development (referral is required if this is evident and has not been assessed by a medical practitioner); current medications (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements and over-the-counter medicines); frequency and method of ear cleaning; drug allergies/adverse drug effects; immunisation status as per the Australian Immunisation Handbook. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients: 'Consider referring to the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual for further information for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients living in rural and remote communities (9).' Reminder: 'Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.'

steps.description: Examination: 'Conduct assessment of vital signs – temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, hydration status.' 'Examine for tender or enlarged cervical lymph nodes.' 'Conduct visual examination and palpation of mastoid area.' 'Exclude red flags.' Ear examination using otoscopy: 'Physical examination including otoscopy of both ears is required to differentiate between diffuse AOE, AOM and other ear conditions (1, 3, 6).' 'Ear examination should be conducted in accordance with the Queensland Health and Royal Flying Doctors Primary Clinical Care Manual. An ear differential diagnosis flowchart is also included (5).' 'Before performing the ear examination, the ear canal must be gently cleaned to remove any discharge with a tissue rolled up to a point (dry mopping) to visualise ear drum (5, 10).' 'The TM must be visualised to confirm a diagnosis of AOM (Refer to Figure 1), although this can be difficult in the presence of extensive otorrhoea (1).' 'If pain levels allow, pneumatic otoscopy may be conducted to check for TM movement: If the TM moves freely back and forward, perforation and fluid in the middle ear (AOM) can generally be excluded. Reduced mobility of an intact TM is a good indication of the presence of middle ear fluid (11).' 'Check for other symptoms if required (nose, throat, cough) (5).'

steps.description: Confirm the diagnosis: 'A red TM or pain alone is not diagnostic of AOM (1).' 'Pain or redness alone is not sufficient to diagnose AOM; pneumatic otoscopy is required to diagnose and exclude other ear conditions with similar presentations (1).' In children, a diagnosis of AOM requires the rapid onset (within 48 hours) of: Pain; Signs of acute inflammation of the TM (TM is bulging and opaque; TM may be red from inflammation or white from pus in the middle ear); Signs of middle ear effusion (Otorrhoea can be indicative of TM perforation and middle ear effusion if acute otitis externa (AOE) has been excluded (1, 4, 5, 7); Otitis media with effusion is characterised by middle ear effusion without other signs and symptoms of AOM, where this is present longer than 3 months is suggestive of persistent otitis media with effusion (glue ear) (1); Otorrhea that has been present for > 2 weeks and a perforation is suggestive of chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) (5)). In adults: 'unilateral symptoms are most common and include mild to severe ear pain and decreased hearing'; an URTI or allergic rhinitis will often precede the onset of AOM (3); other symptoms include dizziness/vertigo (infrequent), systemic symptoms (particularly fever), partial or complete opacification of the TM, or erythema (3); 'the key signs of AOM are bulging and reduced mobility of the TM (3).' Key points (p6): 'AOM is predominantly a childhood infection, however, it may also occur in adults (3). The peak age prevalence is 6-18 months (4).' 'In the majority of paediatric cases, AOM is self-limiting and spontaneously resolves without the requirement for antibiotics (1, 4).'

(b) 'Urgent referral to an emergency department (without concurrent antibiotic therapy) – patient may make their own way to the emergency department:' Recent trauma to the ear or head (this may be associated with hearing loss or balance issues); Severe symptoms or rapidly worsening symptoms including Intense pain or headache, Facial paralysis/palsy, Red, swollen and tender behind the ear (possible acute mastoiditis); Tympanic membrane (TM) 'red flag' signs: Crust/scab or granulation in attic region (discharge/odour may be present), Severely retracted (sucked in) TM or retraction pocket in attic area of eardrum, Dull white mass behind TM, Perforation in attic region, near the edge of the TM or medium to large in size (refer to Figure 2). (c) 'Refer to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate): Urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours (without concurrent antibiotic therapy):' A clear diagnosis of AOM cannot be made; When the TM cannot be visualised. (d) 'Urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours (antibiotic therapy may be provided concurrently):' The patient has otic discharge/otorrhea present; Children with symptoms that worsen or do not improve after 48 hours of regular analgesia and supportive management; Refractory otitis externa with temperature over 390C [as printed]; Cellulitis beyond the ear canal; Granulation tissue or exposed bone in the ear canal; Severe nocturnal otalgia; Purulent otorrhoea; Symptoms are recurrent (3 or more episodes in 6 months or 4 or more episodes in 12 months); The patient has persistent otitis media with effusion (glue ear); Children presenting with signs and symptoms of a complication, or at high risk of complications from AOM (refer to Table 1). (e) 'Children who are prescribed antibiotic therapy must be concurrently referred to a medical practitioner for review.' (f) 'All children at high risk of complications must be referred to a medical practitioner for management. Antibiotic therapy may be provided concurrently to medical practitioner referral where clinically appropriate (1).' (g) TM 'red flag' signs that require immediate referral to a medical practitioner (p11). (h) delayed speech or language development not yet assessed by a medical practitioner. steps.description: Management and treatment plan — Reminder: 'Adequate pain relief is the mainstay of treatment for acute otitis media. Antibiotic therapy is not required for most patients. Antibiotic therapy is commonly inappropriately prescribed and is of limited benefit in most patients (1).' 'Pharmacist management of patients with AOM involvesNB1: supportive management: Aural hygiene and care at home in accordance with The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Fact sheet: Ear infections and glue ear, and the Australian Medicines Handbook: drugs for ear infections (2, 12). If discharge is present, advice and education regarding keeping ears dry and the use of dry mopping with tissue spears. The Queensland Health and Royal Flying Doctors Primary Clinical Care Manual contains a step by step guide for dry mopping (5). pharmacotherapy: Oral analgesia NB2 in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Pharmacological management of acute pain (1). Oral antibiotic therapy NB3 in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Ear, nose and throat infections – Otitis media) (1, 4, 11, 12). Consider immunisation where the patient has not received all routine vaccines in accordance with the Australian Immunisation Handbook.' NB1: 'There is limited evidence to guide the management of AOM in adult patients. The Therapeutic Guidelines state that management of AOM in adults is similar to management in children; adequate and regular analgesia is the primary treatment (13). As with paediatric patients, a shared decision-making approach is required to manage patient expectations of antibiotic treatment (1).' NB2: 'Paracetamol, ibuprofen and naproxen (in preparations containing 250mg or less) can be sold as Schedule 2 medicines.' NB3: 'Antibiotic therapy in paediatric patients should only be commenced in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines and the Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People for children with discharge/otorrhoea (from a small perforation), children with symptoms that have not improved or worsened after 48 hours and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children (13-15). Children who are prescribed antibiotic therapy must be concurrently referred to a medical practitioner for review.' Confirm management is appropriate: 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references including the Otitis Media Guidelines for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People (if applicable) to confirm that the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and breastfeeding.'

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan: 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references, should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use (e.g., dosing); how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment (including recognising patient deterioration); when to return to the pharmacist for clinical review.' 'It is the pharmacist's responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources and information provided to patients (and parents/caregivers if applicable) and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions.' 'The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.' Patient resources (p14): Southern Adelaide Local Health Network - Otitis media (ear infection) information sheet; The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Fact sheet: Ear infections and glue ear (2); Child and Family Health Service (CaFHS); Hearing Australia; Alternative ear health services and resources for Aboriginal children in South Australia (Nunkuwarrin Yunti of South Australia Inc.; U8s Aboriginal Ear Health Program [as printed]; Aboriginal Health Council of SA Ltd: Ear Health – The Deadly Sounds Program; DeadlyKidsSA). General advice (p14): 'AOM symptoms should start to improve within 48 to 72 hours after onset, regardless of whether antibiotic treatment is required, but full resolution of symptoms may take 8 days or longer for effusion (13).'
